units.text: ENUMERATING m-CLUSTERS USING EXCEPTIONAL SEQUENCES
For any Dynkin quiver Q, the number of clusters in the cluster category [3] of any hereditary algebra Λ with valued quiver Q is given by the formula
n i=1 h + d i d i

where h is the Coxeter number of Q and d i = 2, • • • , h are the degrees of the principal Winvariant polynomials where W is the Weyl group of Q.The formula was generalized to m-clusters by Fomin and Reading [9]:
p Λ (m) = n i=1 hm + d i d i .

A remarkable paper by Galashin, Lam, Trinh and Williams [10] gives a uniform proof of this formula.This paper gives another perspective on this formula using exceptional sequences.Namely, we show that the set of ordered m-clusters is in 1-1 correspondence with the set of m-exceptional sequences (Definition 1.2.1).This can be viewed as a refinement of the observation that the leading coefficient of n!p Λ (m) is the number of exceptional sequences:
e Λ = n!h n d i .

This uniform formula for e Λ was first observed by Chapoton [6] and now has several uniform proofs, e.g.[20], [11], [8].This is an old unpublished paper whose main result is being upgraded using a new joint result with Shujian Chen [12].A closely related result of Buan, Reiten and Thomas [4] is discussed in section 3.1.
The original version of this paper had a discussion of probability distributions of terms in exceptional sequences of type A n .This has been removed and is being published as a separate paper [17].
Basic definitions

We recall the definitions and basic properties of exceptional sequences from [7], [23].Over an hereditary algebra Λ, a module M is called exceptional if M is rigid and Schurian where rigid means Ext 1 Λ (M, M ) = 0 and Schurian means End Λ (M ) is a division algebra.[Schurian modules are usually called "bricks."]An exceptional sequence of length ℓ for Λ is a sequence of exceptional modules (E 1 , E 2 , • • • , E ℓ ) so that Hom Λ (E j , E i ) = Ext 1 Λ (E j , E i ) = 0 for i < j ≤ ℓ.The exceptional sequence is called complete if it is of maximal length and this is well known to occur when ℓ = n, the number of nonisomorphic simple Λ-modules.We consider exceptional sequences up to isomorphism where two sequences (E i ), (E ′ i ) are isomorphic if they have the same length and E i ∼ = E ′ i for all i. 1.1.Relative projective terms.In each exceptional sequence we will define certain terms to be "relatively projective."

For any Λ-module M the (right) perpendicular category M ⊥ is defined to be the full subcategory of mod-Λ of all objects X so that Hom Λ (M, X) = 0 = Ext 1 Λ (M, X).The left perpendicular category ⊥ M is defined analogously.From the six-term exact sequence for Hom Λ (M, −) it follows that M ⊥ and ⊥ M are closed under extensions, kernels and cokernels of morphisms between objects.Any full subcategory of mod-Λ having these properties is called a wide subcategory.It is well-known that the perpendicular categories M ⊥ , ⊥ M are finitely generated, i.e., contain a generator.Conversely, if a wide subcategory W of mod-Λ has a generator X then ⊥ X has a generator, say Y , and W = Y ⊥ .Therefore, perpendicular categories are the same as finitely generated wide subcategories of mod-Λ.

A term E j in an exceptional sequence (E 1 , • • • , E ℓ ) will be called relatively projective if it is a projective object of the perpendicular category of the later terms, (E j+1 ⊕ • • • ⊕ E ℓ ) ⊥ .In a complete exceptional sequence, the first term E 1 is always relatively projective since the perpendicular category (E 2 ⊕ • • • ⊕ E n ) ⊥ is semi-simple.If Λ has finite representation type then we define f Λ (x) to be the degree n integer polynomial given by
f Λ (x) := n k=1 e k x k

where e k is the number of complete exceptional sequences in mod-Λ with k relatively projective terms.This polynomial is suitable for computing the number of m-clusters in the m-cluster category of Λ defined below.This polynomial also gives the number of complete exceptional sequences which, following [22], we denote by e Λ = f Λ (1) = e k .

1.2.m-exceptional sequences.Recall that, since Λ is hereditary, the indecomposable objects of the bounded derived category of mod-Λ have the form M [k] where M is an indecomposable Λ-module and k ∈ Z.We say that
M [k] is exceptional if M is an exceptional Λ-module.
The following definition extends an idea from [13].
Definition 1.2.1.For any m ≥ 0 we define an m-exceptional sequence of length ℓ for Λ to be a sequence of exceptional objects
(E 1 , • • • , E ℓ ) in D b (mod-Λ) so that (1) for all j, E j = M j [d j ] where 0 ≤ d j ≤ m, (2
) (M 1 , • • • , M ℓ ) is an exceptional sequence in mod-Λ and
(3) when d j = m, the module M j is relatively projective in the perpendicular category
⊥ .An m-exceptional sequence will be called complete if it has the maximum length ℓ = n.For m = 1, an m-exceptional sequence is called a signed exceptional sequence [13].

It is clear from this definition that, to every exceptional sequence (E 1 , • • • , E ℓ ) with k relatively projective terms, there correspond (m+1) k m ℓ−k m-exceptional sequences since there are m+1 possibilities for d j when M j is relatively projective and only m possibilities otherwise.Therefore, for Λ of finite type, the number of complete m-exceptional sequences is given by
g Λ (m) := n k=1 e k (m + 1) k m n−k = m n f Λ m + 1 m .
We also consider the m-cluster category of Λ [25].This is defined to be the orbit category of the bounded derived category of mod-Λ modulo the functor τ −1 [m]:
C m (Λ) = D b (mod-Λ)/τ −1 [m]
We identify objects of C m (Λ) with their representative in D b (mod-Λ) in the fundamental domain of τ −1 [m] which we take to be
Thus the indecomposable objects of C m (Λ) are represented by M [j] for some indecomposable Λ-module M where 0 ≤ j ≤ m with the additional condition that M is projective when
j = m. Two object X[j], Y [k] in C m (Λ) are compatible if Ext i D b (X[j], Y [k]) = Ext i D b (Y [k], X[j])
= 0 for all i ≥ 1 and they are not isomorphic.Equivalently, either
(1) j < k and Hom Λ (Y,

X) = 0 = Ext 1 Λ (Y, X), (2) j = k and Ext 1 Λ (X, Y ) = 0 = Ext 1 Λ (Y, X) and X ∼ = Y or (3) j > k and Hom Λ (X, Y ) = 0 = Ext 1 Λ (X, Y ), A maximal pairwise compatible set of exceptional objects of C m (Λ) has n objects and is called an m-cluster for Λ.

The first part of the main theorem of this paper, proved in Section 2 below, is the following which generalizes the m = 2 case proved in the preliminary version of [13].This new proof supersedes the one in [13].

Theorem 1.2.2.Let Λ be a finite dimensional hereditary algebra over any field and k, m ≥ 0. Then there is a 1-1 correspondence between (isomorphism classes of ) ordered k-tuples of pairwise compatible objects in the m-cluster category of Λ and (isomorphism classes of ) mexceptional sequences of length k for Λ.

For example, when m = 0, there is only one 0-cluster of size n, namely the set of projective modules.So, there are n! complete 0-exceptional sequences.These are the same as complete exceptional sequences in which every object is relatively projective.It follows that the number of maximal compatible subsets of C m (Λ), the m-clusters, is equal to
1 n! g Λ (m) = m n n! f Λ m + 1 m
The case of greatest interest is when m = 1.The number of cluster for the algebra Λ is
where f Λ (2) is the number of signed exceptional sequences.Some of the facts that we can see immediately from this formula are:
(1) g Λ (−1) = f Λ (0) = 0 (since E 1 is always relatively projective) (2) g Λ (0) = e n = n! (the number of ordered m-clusters for m = 0).
Proposition 1.2.3.All real roots of the polynomial g Λ (x) are between 0 and −1 including −1 and excluding 0.

Proof.If m ≥ 0 then g Λ (m) > 0 since all terms are nonnegative: e k (m + 1) k m n−k ≥ 0 and the k = n term is n!(m + 1) n ≥ n! > 0. If m < −1 then (−1) n g Λ (m) > 0 since all terms are nonnegative and the k = n term is positive.
The second part of the main theorem, also proved in Section 2 is the following.
Proposition 1.2.4.The 1-1 correspondences of Theorem 1.2.2 can be chosen to be compatible with deletion of the first term in the sense that, if
(T 1 , • • • , T k ) corresponds to (E 1 , • • • , E k ), then (T 2 , • • • , T k ) corresponds to (E 2 , • • • , E k ).
1.3.Recursive formula.We will show that the recursive formula for the number of exceptional sequences given in [22] can be modified to give a recursive formula for f Λ (x).
We review briefly the argument from [22] which counts the number of exceptional sequences
e Λ = e k = f Λ (1)

Let Λ be a hereditary algebra of finite type with connected valued quiver Q.The number of vertices of Q, usually denoted n, is the rank of Λ.For each vertex i of Q, let Q(i) be the valued quiver obtained from Q by deleting the vertex i.Then Q(i) has 1, 2 or 3 components.To count the number of exceptional sequences for Q(i) we need the following lemma.

Lemma 1.3.1.[22] Let A, B be hereditary algebras of finite type with rank n A , n B .Then there is a 1-1 correspondence between complete exceptional sequences for A×B and pairs of complete exceptional sequences for A, B together with a shuffling of the two sequences.Thus
e A×B = n A + n B n A e A e B .
Since a term in an exceptional sequence for A × B is relatively projective if and only if it is relatively projective in A or B whichever it comes from, we get the following.
f A×B (x) = n A + n B n A f A (x)f B (x)
The recursive formula for e Λ is:
Proposition 1.3.2. [22]
For Λ of rank n and Coxeter number h we have:
e Λ = n i=1 h 2 e Λ(i)

Proof.(Summarized from [22]) If P i and I j are in the same orbit of the Auslander-Reiten translation τ then the sum of the lengths of the τ orbits of P i and P j is h.Furthermore, for any indecomposable module M in the union of these τ orbits, M ⊥ , P ⊥ i and P ⊥ j are all isomorphic to Λ(i).Since this counts each indecomposable module twice and since every complete exceptional sequence for Λ is given by an indecomposable module M preceded by a complete exceptional sequence for M ⊥ , we get:
2e Λ = 2 M e M ⊥ = h i e Λ(i) .
The formula in the Proposition follows.
In the above proof, in the union of the τ orbits of P i and P j , the proportion of objects which are projective is exactly 2 h .This gives the following.
Corollary 1.3.3.Let Λ, n, h be as above.Then
f Λ (x) = x + h 2 − 1 n i=1 f Λ(i) (x)
or, equivalently,
g Λ (m) = hm + 2 2 n i=1 g Λ(i) (m).
Proof of main theorem
This section gives the statement and proof of the main theorem.
2.1.Statement of main theorem.

Theorem 2.1.1.There is a bijection between the set of isomorphism classes of m-exceptional sequences of length k and the set of isomorphism classes of ordered k-tuples of pairwise compatible objects in the m-cluster category for any finite dimensional hereditary algebra Λ.Furthermore, this bijection is compatible with deletion of the first term in the sense that, if
(E 1 , • • • , E k ) corresponds to (T 1 , • • • , T k ), then (E 2 , • • • , E k ) corresponds to (T 2 , • • • , T k ).

We will set up notation to give an explicit formula for this bijection.We choose one object from every isomorphism class of exceptional Λ-modules.Let E(Λ) denote the set of these objects.For set theoretic purposes we can consider this to be a subset of Z n since every exceptional module M is determined up to isomorphism by its dimension vector dim M ∈ Z n .

For any finitely generated wide subcategory W of mod-Λ (defined in section 1.1), let E(W) = W ∩ E(Λ).Denote by C m (W) the m-cluster category of W. Objects of C m (W) will be represented by elements of the fundamental domain of the functor τ −1 [m] on the bounded derived category of W, as in (1.1).Thus the exceptional objects of C m (W) are (up to isomorphism) X[j] where X ∈ E(W) and 0 ≤ j ≤ m with the additional condition that X is a relative projective object of W when j = m.Let E m (W) denote this set of objects.We call j the level of the object X [j].Let E m j (W) denote the set of objects of E m (W) of level j.In particular, the rank r ≤ n of W is the number of elements of E m m (W).We use the abbreviation E m (Λ) = E m (mod-Λ).We consider the special case W = T ⊥ where T ∈ E(Λ).This is a wide subcategory of rank n − 1.We note that T is uniquely determined by T ⊥ since T is the unique exceptional object of ⊥ (T ⊥ ).
We use the expression exceptional pair for an exceptional sequence of length 2 in mod-Λ.We say that two are equivalent:
(X, Y ) ∼ (Z, W ) if (X ⊕ Y ) ⊥ = (Z ⊕ W ) ⊥ , i.e., if they span the same rank 2 wide subcategory ⊥ (X ⊕ Y ) ⊥ of mod-Λ.
The key lemma.We state the key lemma, which uses the following notation, and show how it proves the main theorem.
For any

T [k] ∈ E m (Λ), let E T [k] ⊆ E m (Λ) denote the set of all X[j] ∈ E m (Λ) which are compatible with T [k]. Recall that A, B are compatible if A ∼ = B and Hom(A, B[s]) = 0 = Hom(B, A[s]) for all s > 0. For A = X[j], B = T [k]
this is equivalent to one of the following.
(1) j < k and (X, T ) is an exceptional pair, (2) j > k and (T, X) is an exceptional pair or (3) j = k and T, X are ext-orthogonal and nonisomorphic in mod-Λ.

Lemma 2.2.1. For any T [k] ∈ E m (Λ) there is a bijection σ T [k] : E m (T ⊥ ) → E T [k] . Furthermore, A, B are compatible in E m (T ⊥ ) if and only if σ T [k] A, σ T [k] B are compatible in E T [k] .

Proof of Theorem 2.1.1 given Lemma 2.2.1.We show that the bijections σ T [k] give bijections θ p : {p-tuples of compatible objects in E m (Λ)} → {m-exceptional sequences of length p for Λ} compatible with deletion of the first term.The bijections θ p are defined recursively as follows.For p = 1 let θ 1 be the identity mapping.Next, take p ≥ 2.
Let (T 1 , • • • , T p ) be an ordered p-tuple of compatible objects in E m (Λ) and let T p = T [k] be the last object.Then, T i for i < p are compatible elements of E T [k] .So, by the lemma,
σ −1 T [k] (T i ) are compatible objects of E m (T ⊥ ). So, σ −1 T [k] (T 1 , • • • , T p−1 ) = (X 1 , • • • , X p−1
) is an ordered (p − 1)-tuple of compatible objects in the wide subcategory T ⊥ of mod-Λ.Since T ⊥ is isomorphic to mod-Λ ′ for some hereditary algebra Λ ′ , by induction on p, we have the bijection
θ p−1 : {(p − 1)-tuples of compatible objects in E m (T ⊥ )} → {m-exc. seq. of length p − 1 for T ⊥ }
which is given by θ p−2 when first terms are deleted.Let
be the corresponding m-exceptional sequence in T ⊥ .Then we define θ p by

θ p (T 1 , • • • , T p ) = (E 1 , • • • , E p−1 , T [k]). Since θ p−2 (T 2 , • • • , T p−1 ) = (X 2 , • • • , X p−1 ), it follows that θ p−1 (T 2 , • • • , T p ) = (E 2 , • • • , E p ) as required. Conversely, let (E 1 , • • • , E p ) be an m-exceptional sequence for Λ. Let E p = T [k]. Then (E 1 , • • • , E p−1 ) is an m-exceptional sequence in T ⊥ and θ −1 p−1 (E 1 , • • • , E p−1 ) = (X 1 , • • • , X p−1 ) is a (p − 1)-tuple of compatible objects in T ⊥ . Applying σ T [k] gives σ T [k] (X 1 , • • • , X p−1 ) = (T 1 , • • • , T p−1 ) a (p−1)-tuple of compatible objects in C m (Λ). So, θ −1 p (E 1 , • • • , E p ) = (T 1 , • • • , T p )

. By construction the maps θ p , θ −1 p are inverse to each other.Since the maps θ p are compatible with deletion of the first term, so are the maps θ −1 p .Thus the key lemma implies the main theorem.

Remark 2.4.1.Any monomorphism X ֒→ T s induces an epimorphism Ext 1 Λ (T s , Z) ։ Ext 1 Λ (X, Z) for any Z since Λ is hereditary.In particular, Ext 1 Λ (X, Z) = 0 for Z ∈ T ⊥ .For X ∈ T ⊥ this implies that X is a relatively projective object of T ⊥ .
